articles.text: As the trucks complete the 10 weeks of removing soil at the Piedmont Community Pool site, contractors are beginning to build a retaining wall for the new pool. The soil work, which began on May 8 and was initially expected to last through June, is now expected to finish by July 14, two weeks behind schedule due to delays on the part of PG&E to disconnect gas and electric lines in the former pool buildings. The contractor, Wickman Development & Construction, is beginning to construct a 385-foot retaining wall, a process that will involve three weeks of grading the site. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that contractors will be digging holes in the wall for utility lines including gas, water, and Comcast for future facilities. Next week the workers will apply a waterproofing substance to the retaining walls, a process which will take one to two weeks. Contractors will then reinforce the retaining wall with rebar and will spray the wall with “shotcrete,” concrete which is applied to the wall through a high-velocity hose. The pool project is still on track to finish by summer next year. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions about the project may contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@griffinstructures.com, or by phone at 415-858-8582. articles.text: The decision about pickleball vs. tennis at Linda Park will inevitably disappoint some; so, how can an ethical decision be made? Utilitarianism suggests that an ethical choice is the one that leads to the greatest good for the greatest number, while avoiding extreme negative impact. When it isn’t possible to make everybody equally happy, it is right to emphasize making most people as happy as possible, while displeasing as few people as little as possible. Dedicated pickleball at Linda would eliminate current part-time availability of 2 non-regulation-sized tennis courts, currently marked inconveniently for dual-sport use. This reduction would be offset by converting the two Hampton courts to tennis-only use. Typical tennis use of the Linda courts involves one set of two players. Pickleball use of the courts often involves 16 simultaneous players, with many more waiting their turn; using this down time spent speaking with friends and neighbors, providing daily civic engagement and connectivity. Four full-size, regulation tennis courts are available 3/4 miles away at the Community Tennis Courts. Nearby Hampton Field offers two regulation-sized courts; re-striping these for tennis would significantly enhance serious tennis play. Tennis often requires advance planning and arrangement with similarly skilled, similarly inclined players; open pickleball play welcomes the young and old, agile and wonky-kneed, skillful and inept, players who arrive with friends, and solitary newcomers hoping to connect. articles.text: Although the trial of full-time pickleball play at the Linda Beach courts was not a topic on the last Recreation Commission agenda, Piedmonters voiced both their support and concerns for nearly an hour during the public comment period at a two-hour meeting on Wednesday, June 21. Among the approximately 20 speakers, most were pickleball players who supported the trial. However, many neighbors countered that city staff and supporters were not adequately addressing the noise created by the play, which impacted their lives daily. Lisa Neville, who lives near the dog park, said, “I am very much affected by the noise of pickleball. It’s being played 12 to 13 hours a day, seven days a week. This involves not only the game itself but all the noise that goes along with it – the yelling, the shouting, the cheering particularly later at night … I’m all for having a good time playing a sport you love, but when it impacts the entire neighborhood it needs to be reimagined.” Neighbor Elane Rehr said that her “major concern among many concerns is that the constant loud noises from pickleball may be having ill effects on the children’s bodies and on their behavior. I taught psychology for 40 years, and stress has major effects on health. Constant loud noises throughout the day can create stress. Stress can create lifelong negative health consequences.” Former Recreation Commission member Christine Free said that although she had never had a noise complaint for the 38 years she’d been living near the courts, the impact of pickleball play was different. “This issue should not be viewed as a popularity contest between pickleball players and neighbors with each side marshaling supporters to show up and be heard. The numbers are overwhelmingly on the players’ side. It’s an issue of fairness and the Commission doing the right thing for the members of the Piedmont community who have a valid position supported by a wide range of scientific acoustical studies and, more importantly, the testimony of its citizens,” Free added. Constance Whitting, whose backyard is 50 feet from the courts, said that although a program for part-time pickleball play may have been acceptable, “seven days a week is way too much. For those of you who are playing, you’ve made a very good presentation as to why pickleball is great, but you only listen to the ‘pock, pock, pock’ while you play. You don’t listen to it nonstop, in your yard, on your deck, in your home, in the kitchen. It even goes to the living room and bedroom, so I need some relief.” Jamie Patterson said, “There’s not quite enough openness around the noise study. We requested the opportunity to have some say or review of what the structure of the [Recreation Commission’s] noise study was going to be prior to it occurring. That request was not granted.” Although the public comments lasted more than 40 minutes, no action was taken by the Recreation Commission because per state law, items not on the agenda for the public meeting of a board or commission may not be acted upon or discussed. The Commission will address the trial of full-time pickleball play at its next meeting, on Wednesday, July 19, when it is expected to make a recommendation regarding future use of the Linda Beach courts, which will then be brought to the City Council. Community members can send questions and comments about the trial to BeachPickleballTrial@piedmont.ca.gov. “The equation shows that you suits are entirely justified in your feelings of moral uncertainty.”

articles.text: Next Wednesday, July 19, the Recreation Commission is expected to make a recommendation regarding the future use of the Linda Beach courts. The sport of pickleball is in a trial period of full-time play at the courts which will conclude at the end of July. Currently the courts are available for organized drop-in pickleball play Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. First-come, firstserved informal drop-in play is available during remaining weekday hours: 9 a.m. to 10 a.m., and 1 p.m. to 9 p.m. (or dusk, whichever comes first). Community members can share their feedback in-person at the meeting, which will be held in the City Council chambers at City Hall (120 Vista Avenue) at 7:30 p.m. on July 19. After a positive response from most responders to a noise survey sent to neighbors of the courts at Hampton Park and Beach four weeks into the trial, the trial period continued for six more months. In January 2020, the city council approved permanent pickleball play during limited hours at Hampton and Beach. On February 15, 2023, the Recreation Commission approved an exclusive pickleball trial at the Beach Field Tennis Courts for five months, from February 27 through July 31. Since the trial began, city staff and the Recreation Commission have received public feedback with nearly 100 in-person comments at public meetings, over 300 emails, and over 800 responses to a recent online community survey on the trial. Many of these comments regard impacts of safety and noise. In response, the city engaged an acoustical consulting firm, Salter, to study noise levels at the Beach courts during and outside of pickleball play hours. Salter’s report, published on July 6 and available at bit.ly/3NK1UTs, concludes that “pickleball noise [does not] exceed standards set forth by the City General Plan or Municipal Code.” Pickleball players at the Linda Beach courts.

articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Planning Commission discussed two programs for increased housing in Piedmont at their meeting on July 10. Included were design standards for multifamily and mixed-use buildings and ADU incentives. Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) Senior Planner Pierce MacDonald told the Commission, “In 2020, the city received a [state] planning grant in the amount of $160,000 and the City Council approved an agreement with Lisa Wise Consulting to begin work on objective design standards for multifamily and mixed use buildings using this grant funding.” Under this proposal, applications for development of multi-family and mixed-use commercial and residential buildings that conform to a set of measurable architectural standards would be approved directly by city staff, without a public hearing. These standards include elements like building placements, facade designs, window and balcony configurations, and location of parking areas. The plans don’t add any new zoning where these buildings could be developed. They apply only to the existing mixed commercial and residential districts in western Piedmont including parts of Grand, Linda, and Highland Avenues, i.e. “generally urban infill areas and less than 1% of the total land area of Piedmont,” said MacDonald. The standards also don’t change existing zoning rules for building density, height, or parking - they just simplify the process for reviewing applications. Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) To make it easier for Piedmont property owners to build new ADUs, MacDonald said that the City developed permit-ready ADU designs. Any of these designs - which are three Tudor, Craftsman, and Mediterranean styles common to homes throughout Piedmont - can be submitted as-is to receive a planning permit from the city, giving applicants a head start on the development process (though construction reports for the site’s slope and soil conditions still need to be created before a building permit is issued). She added that the city also instituted a program at the beginning of 2023 allowing for homeowners to submit ADUs larger than the city’s standard size “in exchange for a deed restriction mandating that if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet ‘very low income’ affordability thresholds set by the Association of Bay Area Governments.” Both the permit-ready ADU styles, and information on building larger ADUs, is available at bit.ly/43hbjHD. Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) Senior Planner Pierce MacDonald told the Commission, “In 2020, the city received a [state] planning grant in the amount of $160,000 and the City Council approved an agreement with Lisa Wise Consulting to begin work on objective design standards for multifamily and mixed use buildings using this grant funding.” Under this proposal, applications for development of multi-family and mixed-use commercial and residential buildings that conform to a set of measurable architectural standards would be approved directly by city staff, without a public hearing. These standards include elements like building placements, facade designs, window and balcony configurations, and location of parking areas. The plans don’t add any new zoning where these buildings could be developed. They apply only to the existing mixed commercial and residential districts in western Piedmont including parts of Grand, Linda, and Highland Avenues, i.e. “generally urban infill areas and less than 1% of the total land area of Piedmont,” said MacDonald. The standards also don’t change existing zoning rules for building density, height, or parking - they just simplify the process for reviewing applications. Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) To make it easier for Piedmont property owners to build new ADUs, MacDonald said that the City developed permit-ready ADU designs. Any of these designs - which are three Tudor, Craftsman, and Mediterranean styles common to homes throughout Piedmont - can be submitted as-is to receive a planning permit from the city, giving applicants a head start on the development process (though construction reports for the site’s slope and soil conditions still need to be created before a building permit is issued). She added that the city also instituted a program at the beginning of 2023 allowing for homeowners to submit ADUs larger than the city’s standard size “in exchange for a deed restriction mandating that if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet ‘very low income’ affordability thresholds set by the Association of Bay Area Governments.” Both the permit-ready ADU styles, and information on building larger ADUs, is available at bit.ly/43hbjHD. Commission meeting By Selen Ozturk Although the trial of full-time pickleball play at the Linda Beach courts was not a topic on the last Recreation Commission agenda, Piedmonters voiced both their support and concerns for nearly an hour during the public comment period at a two-hour meeting on Wednesday, June 21. Among the approximately 20 speakers, most were pickleball players who supported the trial. However, many neighbors countered that city staff and supporters were not adequately addressing the noise created by the play, which impacted their lives daily. Lisa Neville, who lives near the dog park, said, “I am very much affected by the noise of pickleball. It’s being played 12 to 13 hours a day, seven days a week. This involves not only the game itself but all the noise that goes along with it – the yelling, the shouting, the cheering particularly later at night … I’m all for having a good time playing a sport you love, but when it impacts the entire neighborhood it needs to be reimagined.” Neighbor Elane Rehr said that her “major concern among many concerns is that the constant loud noises from pickleball may be having ill effects on the children’s bodies and on their behavior. I taught psychology for 40 years, and stress has major effects on health. Constant loud noises throughout the day can create stress. Stress can create lifelong negative health consequences.” Former Recreation Commission member Christine Free said that although she had never had a noise complaint for the 38 years she’d been living near the courts, the impact of pickleball play was different. “This issue should not be viewed as a popularity contest between pickleball players and neighbors with each side marshaling supporters to show up and be heard. The numbers are overwhelmingly on the players’ side. It’s an issue of fairness and the Commission doing the right thing for the members of the Piedmont community who have a valid position supported by a wide range of scientific acoustical studies and, more importantly, the testimony of its citizens,” Free added. Constance Whitting, whose backyard is 50 feet from the courts, said that although a program for part-time pickleball play may have been acceptable, “seven days a week is way too much. For those of you who are playing, you’ve made a very good presentation as to why pickleball is great, but you only listen to the ‘pock, pock, pock’ while you play. You don’t listen to it nonstop, in your yard, on your deck, in your home, in the kitchen. It even goes to the living room and bedroom, so I need some relief.” Jamie Patterson said, “There’s not quite enough openness around the noise study. We requested the opportunity to have some say or review of what the structure of the [Recreation Commission’s] noise study was going to be prior to it occurring. That request was not granted.” Although the public comments lasted more than 40 minutes, no action was taken by the Recreation Commission because per state law, items not on the agenda for the public meeting of a board or commission may not be acted upon or discussed. The Commission will address the trial of full-time pickleball play at its next meeting, on Wednesday, July 19, when it is expected to make a recommendation regarding future use of the Linda Beach courts, which will then be brought to the City Council. pages.text: Wednesday, July 12, 2023 5 Troop One brings 100 years of history By Samantha R. Pell No one knows the history of Piedmont’s Troop One better than former longtime Troop One Scoutmasters John Stewart and Rich Harms, so I turned to them for a story as rich and juicy as the famed Troop One burgers. Scouting in Piedmont dates back to 1910 under the leadership of Rev. Sturchell, minister of Piedmont Community Church. It was six years before the national organization, Boy Scouts of America, was chartered by Congress. The Piedmont Council was chartered in 1921, and Troop One was its first troop. Troop One prides itself on training leaders and having a strong structure, all while enforcing one of Scouting’s core values of empowering and enabling Scouts, ready for real life situations. Roughly 20 years ago Rich Harms, the Scoutmaster, decided to start a Scout-run fundraiser. At the time the hamburger stand was not so elaborate. Parents brought their own barbecue charcoal, and lighter fluid. It was operated out of a few pop-up tents and was by no means a grand affair. The Troop recognized the need Samantha Pell (left), Brigid Gaffikin, Susannah Cantrill, Eleanor Hawthorn, Dave Larson, Cade Ogles, Ciaren Gallagher, Nicholas Markopolous, and Liam Leahy at Troop One’s annual hamburger stand on the Fourth of July for new equipment, and in true Scouting fashion, came up with an innovative idea – sell hamburgers on the 4th of July at the parade. It soon became the main source of funding. Ready for the lunch rush after the 4th of July Parade, watermelon pieces await hungry parade goers. Earlybird hamburger customers prior to the 4th of July Parade However, other interests were at hand. “We wanted to open an opportunity to have Scouts learn about retail,” explained Stewart, whose e-mail address remains at scoutmaster.stewar t@gmail.com. During his years as Scoutmaster, the stand was expanded with the purchase of four commercial, natural gas grills. Troop One always emphasizes preparing Scouts for their future life, having Scouts portray a positive image of Scouting with the burger stand. Some of the early challenges were getting Scouts to sign up to help. “From the beginning, I made it very clear that the Scouts would have to step up to help,” Stewart said. As previously mentioned, Troop One values leadership and having Scouts step up, take initiative, and lead. One of the many things that makes Troop One unique is that it requires all of its youth leaders to attend the National Youth Leadership Training. It’s an intense, oneweek camp of sorts that “provides a solid training foundation which will assist in training young leaders”. A reminder from Stewart is: “Good leaders are not born, they are trained.” After operating for more than 100 years, raising future leaders is part of Troop One’s DNA. Part of the goal of training leaders ties into the burger stand. Scouts are involved in every step in the preparation, execution, and follow up for the stand. Promoting the stand is one of the largest responsibilities that the Scouts have. In addition to being Piedmont’s first Scout Troop (and possibly first in the country), Troop One can also claim many other firsts. Its hamburger stand was the first Scout-run fundraiser for a troop. In addition, it was the first to start going to Kirby Cove (in Marin near the Golden Gate Bridge) each March to prepare for the busy upcoming camping season. Furthermore, only a few years ago Troop One had no girls whatsoever. After joining as the Troop’s first girl two years ago, two more followed suit. And last spring we had six more girls join. All this goes to show that they can grow, adapt and change rapidly – another core value of Scouting... and life in general. Troop One has been pioneering Scouting for the past 100 years but has never failed to lose sight of what’s important: community. Always ready to step up, it stands out by always volunteering, and giving back. Our burger stand is both a service to the community and a fundraiser, but it’s far more than a fundraiser. It’s an event that celebrates and brings together the Scouts and community. Troop One offers its huge thanks to its burger stand committee of Bernice and Mike Gallagher, Kristen and Tim Ogles, and Siow Fang Tan and James Pell. In addition, it extends thanks to its generous sponsors, Dave Larson of Piedmont Grocery, Teresa Baum of Compass Real Estate, Trader Joe’s of Rockridge, and many parent volunteers. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s College and Career Center will have to find a new Director next year. Gwenly Carrel, its Director for the last four years, has retired. Although she only had a short stint at PUSD, she sat down with the Post to discuss the past, present and future of her career, and college admissions in general. Carrel spent 2002-2014 as the College & Career Advisor at Campolindo High School in Moraga, where she worked with Carol Kitchens, the wife of former Piedmont High principal Rich Kitchens. That connection brought her to Piedmont in 2019, a time of great transformation in college admissions. The biggest event of the year for the College and Career Center is Mock College Admission Night. Just as Carrel was getting ready for the event which helps juniors and underclassmen understand what makes a strong college application, the Covid pandemic hit. It was March 13, 2020. Her first class of seniors, already finished with their college applications, faced the dilemma of deciding which college admission to accept. “[The class of 2020] couldn’t even go on trips to look at the campuses where they were accepted to make their decisions.” Carrell explained. “I would tell them you can at least go there and drive around the campus. The poor class of 2021 was just starting, and they couldn’t go look at things. They couldn’t put their lives together,” she added. Then the University of California got rid of standardized testing. “Why did that happen? Could you go to a SAT or ACT testing center? Gwenly Carrel, its Director for the last four years, has retired. Just as Carrel was getting ready for the event which helps juniors and underclassmen understand what makes a strong college application, the Covid pandemic hit. It was March 13, 2020. Parents were sending College and Career Center’s Gwenly Carrel retires the landscape of college admissions, however. “There were so many changes along the way in 20 years. But in second-half stoppage time, Canada was awarded a penalty kick after the ball came into contact with Miles Robinson’s hand. Canada nearly stole the match when Jacob Shaffelburg scored in the 109th minute, but with six minutes left in overtime, the U.S. scored on an own goal by Canada’s Scott Kennedy. Goalkeeper Dayne St. Clair’s attempted clearance bounced off Kennedy and into the net. It with the game now tied at 2-2, the game went to penalty kicks to provide a winner. U.S. keeper Matt Turner stopped Canada’s first two penalty shots, and San Jose Earthquakes’ Cade Cowell put the U.S. ahead, 3-2. Penalties are typically converted at an 80 percent success rate, making Turner one of the most successful PK defenders in world football. JOSH BERNSTEIN Distance Swimmer Piedmont High Class of 1975 University of California Class of 1979 Josh Bernstein, PHS Class of 1975, is a lifelong swimmer who, at the age of 66, just finished one of the most prestigious open-water swims in the world, On June 29 he crossed the 21-mile English Channel with a group of six swimmers, finishing the crossing in 13 hours, 58 minutes. He’s done countless endurance swims, including swimming the width of Lake Tahoe, from Alcatraz to San Francisco numerous times, and recently the aquatic Bay to Breakers, from the Bay Bridge past the Golden Gate Bridge to Ocean Beach on June 10. across the English Channel in the June 6 edition of the Piedmont Post. Below, he highlights his training schedule and his approach to swimming and athletics. What is your workout program this summer? I get up at 4:00 am and drive to San Francisco so I’m at the South End Rowing Club by 5:15 or so. I do a gym workout that includes a lot of stretching, joint support, and strengthening. Then, our Swiss Pod gets in the Bay promptly at 6:16 a.m. – yes, precisely 6:16! We typically swim for about an hour. Where we go is entirely dependent on the tides and other conditions. On weekends we get in at 7:27 and go longer. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Now that my big swims are behind me, I’m focusing on strengthening, nutrition, and trimming down a bit, along with constantly working on my swimstroke. How are you measuring your development? I’ve long since abandoned that sort of thing. I spent decades watching the clock and counting mileage. Now, I swim for fun. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? One of my podmates, Rick Mulvihill, spent his career coaching. He keeps an eye on my technique and he pushes me to improve. When I’m training for a big event, I check in with some of my previous coaches I’m still in touch with. I’m also friends with some pretty amazing open water swimmers like Lynne Cox and Suzanne Heim-Bowen, who generously offer helpful suggestions. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Starting last November, I completed a 5-mile swim in pretty cold water from Kirby Cove to Aquatic Park. Then in May I swam another cold 5-miler, the “5 Coves of Death.” In early June, I swam the 10-mile “Bay to Breakers” from the Bay Bridge out the Golden Gate then south to Ocean Beach. Swim Across America raises money for UCSF Children’s Hospital for cancer research and treatment by swimming from St. Francis Yacht Club to Aquatic Park. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Wimbledon.com Mackie McDonald, a former Piedmont High tennis star, competed at Wimbledon on July 3. Mackie McDonald’s entry at Wimbledon was more brief than desired. He lost in the first round to No. 23 seeded Alexander Bublik on July 3, Scores of the fourset match were close all the way, 6-7 (7-3), 6-4, 6-4, 6-4. It was an rough result for Mackie after winning the first set and leading the third at 3-0, but Bublik found his rhythm and carried the momentum throughout the remaining sets. The result brings McDonald’s world-ranking to No. 53. He was ranked No. 48 in August last year. Bublik is currently No. 30 on the ATP World Tour. Although he took the final three sets, it was a battle all the way until the finish. McDonald and Bublik traded games in the second set as the server until Bublik pulled ahead by winning the fifth game as the returner. McDonald led 4-1 in the third set, but Bublik won five straight games to pull ahead. In the final set, Bublik jumped out to a 3-1 lead and although Mackie made things closer at a 5-4 deficit, Bublik took match point as the server. Bublik largely took over the match with his effectiveness in serves, recording 24 aces on the afternoon. McDonald, meanwhile, only recorded six. He also had a loss in the first round at the French Open on May 28 to No. 24 seeded Sebastian Korda in three sets, 6-4, 7-5, 6-4. Korda, a 22-year-old American, entered as the world’s No. 30 ranked player and is now No. 25. McDonald led the first set 3-2, but conceded three straight games to fall behind 5-3. He won the next game as the server to make it closer 5-4, but Korda won setpoint after going up 40-15. In the second set, McDonald led 4-3 but Korda tied 4-4 as the server and went ahead 5-4 as the returner. McDonald tied it 5-5 by taking a break point of his own, but Korda won as the returner, once again, 6-5. With set-point, McDonald initially led 30-15, but Korda wound up winning the next two points to win 40-30. In the third set, Mackie the two traded games until McDonald led 4-3, but Korda tied 4-4, then won his fifth game as the returner before closing out in service winning in deuce for match point. McDonald had an opportunity to win while holding Advantage as the returner, but Korda effectively responded. The Wimbledon is the grass court portion of the Grand Slam tournament schedule. McDonald now looks ahead to his strongest season, the hard court season that stretches from July to November. Mackie will next compete in the U.S. Open in New York City from August 28–September 4. But it is a highly competitive race, with Slovenian rider Tadej Pogačar in second place just 17 seconds behind. Vingegaard established a 25-second lead on Pogačar following Stage 6 and continued the advantage through Stage 9’s mountain course to Puy de Dôme, where the Slovenian trimmed eight seconds from the Dane’s lead. This year’s race has been a terrific tour for American rider Nielson Powless, who currently has a good lead in the mountain climber classification with 46 points, ahead of Felix Gall of Austria with 28 points. Fellow American, Sepp Kuss, is in 10th place, but he’s playing a support role to leader Vingegaard as a member of the Jumbo-Visma team. Le Tour progresses through a flat Stage 11 today, July 12, and a medium mountain run for Stage 12 on Thursday, July 13. That’s when the tour begins three straight mountain stages before a rest day on July 17, followed by a Stage 16 time trial and another mountain course for Stage 17. The Stage 13 mountain ride occurs on Bastille Day, France’s Independence Day, traveling 86 miles from Châtillon sur Chalaronne to Grand Colombier. It features two steep ascents, including a summit finish on Grand Colombier via a 17.4 kilometer climb at a 7.1 percent grade. Stage 14 is a 94-mile ride from Annemasse to Morzine with six Photo courtesy of Eurosport Jonas Vingegaard, the defending 2022 Tour de France champion, returned to the lead in General Classification following Stage 6. Photo courtesy of Nielson Powless official Twitter American rider Nielson Powless currently leads the mountain rider classification. different climbing sections and varying ascents and descents along the way. The ride opens with a 4.2- kilometer climb at a 4.6 percent grade up Col de Saxel, followed by a seven-kilometer ride up Col de Cou at a grade of 7.4. From there, they will climb 5.8 kilometers up Col de Feu at a steep 7.8 percent. After a brief 1,029 meter climb up Col de Jambaz, the tour then has two long climbs. They will go 13.9 kilometers up Col de la Ramaz at 7.1 percent and then have one more 11.6 kilometer ride up Col de Joux Plane at a killer 8.5 percent grade. It equates for a total elevation gain of over 14,000 feet. Stage 15 is another 14,000- plus foot day of elevation gain and a grueling 111 miles. The stage’s three marquee climbs go 7.2 kilometers up Col de la Forclaz at a 7.3 percent grade. From there, the tour turns 11.3 kilometers up Col de la Croix Fry, another 7 percent grade. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s production Out of Character is playing onstage now through July 30. Tony Award-winner Ari’el Stachel, director for Out of Character, is an Israeli American of Yemeni Jewish descent living in Berkeley. This new single-character show follows Stachel’s attempts to hide his Middle Eastern background post 9/11 as a young adult. Stachel joins former Berkeley Rep artistic director Tony Taccone to tell his story in his new solo show. Out of Character looks at the intersections of race, mental health and survival. articles.text: John Krasinski directed, co-wrote and starred in A Quite Place A Quiet Place is almost totally without dialogue, but still conveys a sense of dread more loudly than the familiar horror trope so common with this genre. It is a film of faces, close-ups, capturing a spectrum of deep familial affection to unequivocal terror. It is brilliant in its premise – simple and elegant. The opening scene tells us it is DAY 89. Immediately it is evident that something terrible has taken place, an apocalypse of a kind. The what, and how is unclear. The place is a small, bucolic town in upstate New York. A family (three children and their mother and father) is scavenging the pillaged shelves of a grocery/drug store searching for supplies and medicine. They walk slowly, carefully, each is barefooted, no one speaks or makes a sound. They speak to one another not in hushed whispers but in sign language. Within minutes the tension that will haunt the film throughout is palpable. What is the source of their fear? When they leave the store they walk, inexplicably, on a ribbon of sand that cushions their footsteps. The parents, Lee and Evelyn Abbott (John Krasinski and Emily Blunt), are hyper-vigilant, pausing to listen. Whatever is out there represents an existential threat in the extreme; only the audience is not given even a hint of what it might be. Not until there is a moment that is completely unexpected, involving only a flash of movement, resulting in the couple’s youngest being taken. Lee’s face is twisted in anguish as he runs toward his son, realizing he is too late to save him. What was a blindingly quick reveal is followed by the screen informing us that more than 400 days have passed and we see a Victorian farmhouse that has been turned into a survivalist island. It is inviting, cozy even, surrounded by crops, powered by a generator, a necklace of lights at night are strung form the house to the outbuildings. A wide path of sand leads to the front porch. Thus far, by what we see, we’re told that this family has endured. Actually, they have thrived, for we also notice that Evelyn is pregnant. In the basement, in Lee’s gear-laden workshop, are electronics and multiple screens monitoring the exterior. On one wall are newspapers with headlines warning people to avoid all sound. There’s a shortwave radio on a work bench. The house is filled with light, for apparently whatever “they” are, they cannot see, only hear, even the faintest crunch of a dried leaf beneath a carelessly placed foot. A frequent gesture, universal in its understanding, is an index finger placed in front of the lips, conveying most often to the children that above all, in that moment, silence is their only defense. Remain still, hushed, wait, listen, their very lives depend on it. Even when the family spends an evening playing Monopoly, the pips are covered with material. I’m hesitant to continue to reveal anything more than what is evident in the first act. This is a film that must be seen fresh. To know any more would diminish what are emotions of trepidation and uncertainty, wrapped in a plot that grows and unravels silently, step-by-step, so-to-speak. All of this film is completely authentic and believable – though a certain suspension of disbelief is required. The family is impossible not to care about. We wish above all that no harm will come to them; it’s an investment in the characters that is impossible not to make. A Quiet Place is a title that seems benign. It isn’t. As a film, it is a harrowing allegory. What is out there is vague and predatory and beyond comprehension. In other words, Krasinski, along with his co-writers, Bryan Woods and Scott Beck, handle all aspects of this very excellent film with artistry and finesse, implicitly understanding that less can be more when dealing with imagination. A Quiet Place. Directed by John Krasinski. Starring John Krasinski, Emily Blunt, Millicent Simmonds. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on VUDU/Ptime/Paramont+.
articles.title: A Quiet Place – surviving an apocalypse

articles.text: The power of fine filmmaking can be extraordinary: take the issue of illegal immigration, generally regarded in the abstract – our borders are porous, hence there are 11 million undocumented workers in America. It is a problem that is distant, political, a conundrum and one from which we are often insulated. But create an irresistible story about a gardener, Carlos Galindo (Demian Bichir), living in East Los Angeles, without documents, a single parent raising a 16-yearold boy, Luis (Jose Julian), and suddenly the problem becomes real, even personal. At the center of this splendid film is a principled man, cutting and trimming the grounds of the wealthy, while struggling to keep himself and Luis above water. His goal, his dream, is to have his own truck, his own tools and mower, and to create a life that has at its center, family and stability. A Better Life is a moving portrait of Carlos, who leaves his one-bedroom bungalow each morning at dawn and returns long after dark, falling exhausted onto the hard-used sofa in the living room. He is unaware that his son is drifting away, who finds the faux family security of gangs more inviting than the home offered by his father. Luis, who was born in America, stands with one foot in the culture of his parents and one foot in the culture he finds at school and on the street. His connection to Mexico is tentative, the language and customs seeming ever more strange. Each day Carlos copes with anxiety because of his illegal status, ever fearful that he will be stopped by “la migra” and asked for some form of identification. When the gardener he works for announces that he is returning to Mexico and offers to sell him his truck and include his client list. Carlos, who has no license and no I.D., decides to take the risk. He views the truck as the path to what he calls the American dream. Filled with pride, he drives through Los Angeles, looking out the window of the truck. He sees parts of the city that are hidden from the usual traveler. Sadly, many of the inhabitants, though they contribute to America, are part of a shadow population that is seen but not seen, residing in a place apart, living in immigration ghettos with drapes tightly closed. But just as Carlos senses that life is about to turn around, events occur that put him and his son in jeopardy. Know that A Better Life is not a political tract nor a polemic about immigration. It is a deeply human story, both touching and compelling, about a father and his son who learn about one another as they set about recovering something they have lost. Their journey is transformative. A Better Life. Directed by Chris Weitz. Starring Demian Bichir, Jose Julian, and Dolores Heredia. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: A Better Life a well-made film of quest for the American dream

At the center of this splendid film is a principled man, cutting and trimming the grounds of the wealthy, while struggling to keep himself and Luis above water. His connection to Mexico is tentative, the language and customs seeming ever more strange. Each day Carlos copes with anxiety because of his illegal status, ever fearful that he will be stopped by “la migra” and asked for some form of identification. When the gardener he works for announces that he is returning to Mexico and offers to sell him his truck and include his client list. Carlos, who has no license and no I.D., decides to take the risk. He views the truck as the path to what he calls the American dream. Filled with pride, he drives through Los Angeles, looking out the window of the truck. He sees parts of the city that are hidden from the usual traveler. Sadly, many of the inhabitants, though they contribute to America, are part of a shadow population that is seen but not seen, residing in a place apart, living in immigration ghettos with drapes tightly closed. But just as Carlos senses that life is about to turn around, events occur that put him and his son in jeopardy. Know that A Better Life is not a political tract nor a polemic about immigration. It is a deeply human story, both touching and compelling, about a father and his son who learn about one another as they set about recovering something they have lost. It is a film of faces, close-ups, capturing a spectrum of deep familial affection to unequivocal terror. It is brilliant in its premise – simple and elegant. The opening scene tells us it is DAY 89. Immediately it is evident that something terrible has taken place, an apocalypse of a kind. The what, and how is unclear. The place is a small, bucolic town in upstate New York. A family (three children and their mother and father) is scavenging the pillaged shelves of a grocery/drug store searching for supplies and medicine. They walk slowly, carefully, each is barefooted, no one speaks or makes a sound. They speak to one another not in hushed whispers but in sign language. Within minutes the tension that will haunt the film throughout is palpable. What is the source of their fear? When they leave the store they walk, inexplicably, on a ribbon of sand that cushions their footsteps. The parents, Lee and Evelyn Abbott (John Krasinski and Emily Blunt), are hyper-vigilant, pausing to listen. Whatever is out there represents an existential threat in the extreme; only the audience is not given even a hint of what it might be. Not until there is a moment that is completely unexpected, involving only a flash of movement, resulting in the couple’s youngest being taken. Lee’s face is twisted in anguish as he runs toward his son, realizing he is too late to save him. What was a blindingly quick reveal is followed by the screen informing us that more than 400 days have passed and we see a Victorian farmhouse that has been turned into a survivalist island. It is inviting, cozy even, surrounded by crops, powered by a generator, a necklace of lights at night are strung form the house to the outbuildings. A wide path of sand leads to the front porch. Thus far, by what we see, we’re told that this family has endured. Actually, they have thrived, for we also notice that Evelyn is pregnant. In the basement, in Lee’s gear-laden workshop, are electronics and multiple screens monitoring the exterior. On one wall are newspapers with headlines warning people to avoid all sound. There’s a shortwave radio on a work bench. The house is filled with light, for apparently whatever “they” are, they cannot see, only hear, even the faintest crunch of a dried leaf beneath a carelessly placed foot. A frequent gesture, universal in its understanding, is an index finger placed in front of the lips, conveying most often to the children that above all, in that moment, silence is their only defense. Remain still, hushed, wait, listen, their very lives depend on it. Even when the family spends an evening playing Monopoly, the pips are covered with material. I’m hesitant to continue to reveal anything more than what is evident in the first act. This is a film that must be seen fresh. To know any more would diminish what are emotions of trepidation and uncertainty, wrapped in a plot that grows and unravels silently, step-by-step, so-to-speak. All of this film is completely authentic and believable – though a certain suspension of disbelief is required. The family is impossible not to care about. We wish above all that no harm will come to them; it’s an investment in the characters that is impossible not to make. A Quiet Place is a title that seems benign. It isn’t. As a film, it is a harrowing allegory. What is out there is vague and predatory and beyond comprehension. In other words, Krasinski, along with his co-writers, Bryan Woods and Scott Beck, handle all aspects of this very excellent film with artistry and finesse, implicitly understanding that less can be more when dealing with imagination. articles.text: Richard Madden and Lily James in Disney’s live-action remake of Cinderella If you see the title of the recently released Cinderella and shrug, feeling the story is all too familiar, wondering what could possibly be new in this narrative. Know that you have not seen the story presented in this surprising and beautiful way. And once again done by Disney. This is a contemporary version of an iconic fairytale, fresh and engaging (with a tweak here by the writers), but not surprising given that it’s directed by the talented Kenneth Branagh. The story, in essence, is simple and direct, and unlike those that have come before (the most memorable being the animated version by Disney some 65 years ago), relies very little on special effects or CGI. There is, out of necessity, the scene when Ella’s Fairy Godmother (Helena Bonham Carter) appears and turns a simple pumpkin into a startlingly beautiful, ornate coach, and the house mice slowly morph into six white steeds and two lizards become the coachmen. In the main, and to its credit, this film is character driven, and the wonder of Cinderella can be found in watching each individual revealed – from the very kind and enchanting Ella (Lilly James), to the cruel and sadistic Lady Tremaine (Cate Blanchett). The set up for the movie takes almost all of act one to construct. Ella is living an idyllic life with her mother (Hayley Atwell) and father (Ben Chaplin) in a gorgeous English countryside mansion. She is embraced by her loving family and secure in her place as a much cared for daughter. Unexpectedly, Ella’s mother falls suddenly ill and dies, leaving Ella with just her father. Time passes, years slip by, and he decides to remarry, choosing a benign widow (or so he believes), Lady Tremaine, who has two daughters Ella’s age, Drisella and Anastasia (Sophia McShera and Holliday Granger). With their arrival, Ella’s life changes as act two unfolds. At first she is tolerated by her stepmother, and mocked by the sisters. But when her father dies on a business trip, Ella, now orphaned, finds her position in the household one in which she is ostracized and turned into a servant, relegated to the attic, always at the beck and call of the three women. It is they who name her Cinderella, for she sleeps by the den fireplace because the attic is too cold in winter. And so the story blossoms in a most compelling and captivating manner. The king (Derek Jacobi) announces that he will give a magnificent royal ball. His young son (Richard Madden), the heir and prince, insists that all of the single maidens of the kingdom must be invited. As it turns out, the prince is about to choose a bride at the ball, whether she is a commoner or titled. Naturally, Tremaine forbids Cinderella from going. That is until there is a magical moment when the tale soars. It is both glorious to watch and touching in its emotions, none of which are disguised behind computer trickery. The visuals – and they are stunning – create a magnetism that transcends and surprises, even though the outcome is solidly based on the Disney idea of “happily ever after.” It is in getting to that moment that separates this Cinderella from all its precursors (and there have been many, to include a TV special starring Julie Andrews). As an aside, just before Ella’s mother dies, she takes her daughter’s hand and asks her to always have courage and above all else, be kind, a moral principle that Ella tries to live by, and one that is woven with sensitivity into the story. Ella is, indeed, courageous and reflexively kind no matter the abuse heaped upon her by the mean-spirited Tremaine. She is also by nature innocent; but also tenacious and someone who, in every frame, is believable as she demonstrates how deeply her decency frames her life. It’s a wonderfully resonant message, brought to you once again by Disney, who has always chosen to see the world not as it is but as it should be. Cinderella. Directed by Kenneth Branagh. Starring Lily James, Cate Blanchett and Richard Madden. Disney-Live action. 1 hr., 45 min, Rated PG. Released 2015, Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Wow. Kids are going to love How to Train Your Dragon. Let’s start with an inspired, breathtaking scene: a young Viking named Hiccup, seated securely on the back of Toothless, an ebony dragon, soars through the clouds in a prolonged flight. The colors are lush and gorgeous, the sky a startlingly blue in contrast to the enormous cumulus clouds. Hiccup, eyes wide, is both exhilarated and terrified. This scene, like so many in this film, is testimony to the depth and breadth of the imagination of the filmmakers, and illustrates how state-of-the-art animation, combined with the technology of 3-D, has made quantum strides in the last several years. Of course, neither technology nor 3-D can save a film if the story lacks serious mojo. How to Train Your Dragon has all the right stuff: a sweet if recognizable story that will resonate with kids ages nine and above. And the characters are, to a person, perfect. Briefly, there’s young Hiccup (Jay Baruchel), the son of Stoick the Vast (Gerard Butler), who lives on a small island, Berk, off the coast of Scotland. For 300 years dragons have been attacking their village, making off with their livestock. The Vikings have fought back and along the way developed an abiding hatred for and fear of dragons. Hiccup, a newbie adolescent, rebelling against his chieftain father and his community, resists learning to fight dragons. Stoick is both frustrated and angry with his son. Clearly Hiccup, lean in stature (the Vikings are all more than hefty), and not inclined to fight back when the dragons attack, is not cut out to be a dragon slayer. This becomes all too clear when, wandering in the forest, he comes across a fallen dragon, Toothless. Instead of killing the dragon he befriends him. And that budding friendship sets the story in motion. Hiccup not only helps Toothless regain his ability to fly (he designs and makes him a prosthetic tail) with the assistance of Astrid (America Ferrera), a wonderful tween-teen-tomboy (first it’s boy meets dragon, then it’s boy meets girl). They begin to work out a plan that will change the attitudes of the village toward dragons. Hiccup soon discovers that he and Astrid are not alone. With the help of his friends – Tuffnut, Fishlegs, Snotlout – they transform the future of Beck. What is also so much fun is that the dragons are marvelous – Hideous Zippleback, Monstrous Nightmare and the uberdragon, Night Fog. As well, all the kids speak in hip teen vernacular (“Vikings have stubbornness issues”), absent the brogue of his father and Gobber the Belch, and they dress like they buy their clothes from the Gap’s Viking annex, to include Ugg boots. Very cool. Astrid has a nifty hairstyle, leggings, short skirt and tons of ‘tude. They’re a goofy but delightful group and youngsters will identify with them and their situation. So, if the gremlins are hanging out this weekend complaining there is nothing to do, suggest How to Train Your Dragon. They might not remember to thank you, but they will enjoy themselves. And so will you. How to Train Your Dragon. Animated. Directed by Christopher Sanchez. Starring Jay Barnchel, Gerard Butler, America Ferrera. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated PG. Released 2010. Streaming on Prime/VUDU/Net Flix/Apple tv.

articles.text: Bruce Conte was an R&B and funk and jazz guitarist known for his performances with Tower of Power from 1972 to 1979. Born in 1950 in Sanger, California, he grew up in Fresno. He and his cousin Victor Conte began playing in a family R&B band in high school in the early 1960s. At first, Bruce played bass, then switched to guitar. Through high school they performed in the rhythm sections of local bands, including Common Ground, playing the local club scene from 1967 to 1969. Conte’s musical influences included Maceo Parker, Dyke and the Blazers, Jimmy Nolan (guitarist with James Brown), Albert King, George Benson and Grant Green. In 1969, Conte moved to the Bay Area and joined the Loading Zone, with vocalist Linda Tillery and organist Tom Coster (from Santana’s band). At Conte’s Loading Zone audition, bassist Doug of the Santana band said, “This guy totally locks in with the drums, he’s obviously the cat.” Bruce Conte was one of the greatest soul/funk rhythm guitar players ever and was an expressive and unique soloist. You’ll recognize him in just a few notes. Around that time, Bruce would sit in at the basement jam sessions at La Val’s Pizza in Berkeley with blues/soul musicians Charlie Musselwhite (harmonica, vocals), Clay Cotton (piano), Terry Hanck (sax, vocals) and others. The Loading Zone gig led to Bruce’s joining Tower of Power. The Loading Zone shared rehearsal space with them and regularly opened for them. In 1972 Castillo changed the TOP lineup and hired Conte, saxophonist Lenny Pickett and vocalist Lenny Williams, all from the Loading Zone. Bruce became close to Tower of Power’s founder and songwriter, Emilio Castillo and the other primary TOP songwriter Stephen Kupka. Conte began co-writing songs with them, occasionally sitting in with the band. With Conte, drummer David Garibaldi, bassist Rocco Prestia, and organist Chester Thompson, Tower of Power formed a ground-breaking rhythm section that influenced countless musicians world-wide. Conte remained with Tower of Power until 1979, performing on the group’s seven albums from Tower of Power to Live And In Living Color. With TOP, Bruce mainly played his 1957 Gibson Les Paul Goldtop with a pickup on the neck and his 1967 Super Reverb amp in the studio and a Quad Reverb or Twin Reverb for live gigs. In 2006 Conte rejoined TOP, touring with the band for 14 months, before moving to Cebu

In 1969, Conte moved to the Bay Area and joined the Loading Zone, with vocalist Linda Tillery and organist Tom Coster (from Santana’s band). At Conte’s Loading Zone audition, bassist Doug of the Santana band said, “This guy totally locks in with the drums, he’s obviously the cat.” Bruce Conte was one of the greatest soul/funk rhythm guitar players ever and was an expressive and unique soloist. You’ll recognize him in just a few notes. Around that time, Bruce would sit in at the basement jam sessions at La Val’s Pizza in Berkeley with blues/soul musicians Charlie Musselwhite (harmonica, vocals), Clay Cotton (piano), Terry Hanck (sax, vocals) and others. The Loading Zone gig led to Bruce’s joining Tower of Power. The Loading Zone shared rehearsal space with them and regularly opened for them. In 1972 Castillo changed the TOP lineup and hired Conte, saxophonist Lenny Pickett and vocalist Lenny Williams, all from the Loading Zone. Bruce became close to Tower of Power’s founder and songwriter, Emilio Castillo and the other primary TOP songwriter Stephen Kupka. Conte began co-writing songs with them, occasionally sitting in with the band. With Conte, drummer David Garibaldi, bassist Rocco Prestia, and organist Chester Thompson, Tower of Power formed a ground-breaking rhythm section that influenced countless musicians world-wide. Conte remained with Tower of Power until 1979, performing on the group’s seven albums from Tower of Power to Live And In Living Color. With TOP, Bruce mainly played his 1957 Gibson Les Paul Goldtop with a pickup on the neck and his 1967 Super Reverb amp in the studio and a Quad Reverb or Twin Reverb for live gigs. In 2006 Conte rejoined TOP, touring with the band for 14 months, before moving to Cebu Guitarist Bruce Conte in the Philippines. In 2012 Conte announced in Los Angeles that he had leukemia. A fund for his medical treatment was established via the Jeremy Wilson Foundation. Bruce died of leukemia nine years later, on August 8, 2021. articles.text: Part 65 in a biweekly series Good landscape design is very much like the good architectural design we spoke of last time. Before anything else, there needs to exist an overall strong concept that is pervasive throughout and is supported by all the components. This basic requirement is fundamental and logical to my way of thinking, but it is often neglected. What we often see as a result is a collection of pieces, or components, that don’t “work together” aesthetically or functionally rather than a comprehensive whole. Each landscape design in our built environment contains any number of design components: paving, grading, fences, gates, retaining walls, outdoor furniture, lighting, signage and of course planting. How these pieces are treated by the landscape architect and then assembled together determines not only the landscaping style and character, but also its overall quality. These components can be derived from many sources including historical models, or from common usage, or simply by fashion (which is quite common). And like all of landscape architecture, there is a melding of use and appearance. There is a function for most all components to accommodate as well as an aesthetic to express. Landscape architectural design evaluation ultimately requires a review of the totality of the components together – the coordination of and synergy between all of the parts – the complete project. But just as the entire detailed landscape project can’t be envisioned and designed all at once, it is helpful in the design process and in judging quality to evaluate the separate design components themselves – to work with the more manageable separate parts, as we often do in this column. It is sometimes difficult to articulate why we like or dislike certain design components and why they are considered good or bad. articles.text: If you read last week’s column you can skip the first two paragraphs. Recently the Sonoma County Vintners Association put on a huge tasting at Kendall-Jackson Winery in Santa Rosa. The “Taste of Sonoma” event was one of the largest and most interesting wine events I have ever participated in. Over 100 wineries from all over the county were pouring their wines often 5 or 6 different wines per provider. The quality was astonishingly high as I had come to expect from Sonoma County. After many years of living in the shadow of its big brother Napa County I feel Sonoma has really come into its own. Certainly, in terms of the experience of wine touring. When friends come to visit, I never take them to Napa to taste. It has become wildly expensive and terribly crowded. Better to ramble around the scenic roads of Sonoma County looking for gems. One thing that was evident from this tasting is that Pinot has hit it big. The grape was everywhere with most regions of the county producing it extensively. Pinot was closely followed by Chardonnay by far the most popular white grape. Throw in some fine Zinfandels, Cabernets and Syrahs and the result was an exceptional and varied day of tasting. The following wines and the ones I reviewed in Part One represent the best of the tasting and even more, represent the best of Sonoma County. • 2021 Arista Pinot Noir Russian River Valley This is a very natural wine bottled unfiltered and unfined. It has a pale to medium ruby color and spicy notes of baking spices, earth, and leather over a core of red and black berry fruit. The medium bodied palate is elegant and nuanced with spicy character and a grainy, fresh frame, continuing to blossom on a long, detailed finish. These wines are made to age and should improve for a decade in the cellar. • 2021 Sangiacomo Pinot Noir Sonoma Coast Sourced from five different vineyards, the Sangiacomo Pinot Noir has singular, alluring scents of violets, rose petals, cranberries and red cherries- this is incredibly layered, deep and detailed. The medium-bodied palate is packed with plum fruit, spices, earth and amaro layers, supported by a fine grain and seamless freshness, finishing long and layered. A great effort. • 2021 Bricoleur Pinot Noir Founder’s Block This is the second release from Bricoleur vineyards. It has a medium ruby color and scents of cranberries, forest floor and spice. It’s light bodied, smoothly textured but firm, with great freshness to lift the savory finish. Perfect accompaniment to beef bourguignon. • 2020 Pride Claret Reserve The Pride vineyard straddles the county line and this wine is 81% Sonoma and 19% Napa fruit. The cepage is 72% Merlot and 28% Cabernet Sauvignon. The Pride Claret has aromas of cassis, blueberry, tobacco, earth with floral notes. Medium-bodied, seamless and fleshy bursting with black fruit, it’s a layered, concentrated wine with rich tannins and a long, savory finish. This is only going to get better in the cellar. 2021 Arista Pinot Noir Russian River Valley Owners of Thirty-Seven Wines pouring their wines.

Direct baking (no water bath) works, but the bread pudding’s bottom and sides will brown and form a crust. Bread pudding is traditionally served with a crème anglaise. A super-premium ice cream has the same ingredients, so a shortcut is melting some ice cream. articles.text: It was the 5th of July, the weather was cloudy and cool, and there was a large turnout of 46 walkers and two K-9 best friends at the Exedra for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays. Karin Fetherston was interested in the historic ceiling panels in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School, and arranged for Pete Palmer, the school district’s Director of Facilities to meet the walkers at the and provide some history. Pete told the walkers about the ceiling, as well as needed repairs that were done to the building. Piedmont’s first public elementary school was built in 1910 and opened its doors in 19 . It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land donor. The school was expanded under the New Deal in the 1930s. After the school board gained funding from the Public Works Administration (PWA) in 1933, work on a new five-classroom wing and an auditorium on the eastern edge of the school began in 1936. The classrooms were built in 1937-38 and the auditorium was added in 1940-42. It was named in honor of Ellen Driscoll, the school’s first principal, who taught at the school for 20 years. The ceiling panels were painted by students in the fifth and sixth grade in a paint-by-number fashion before they were applied to the ceiling. The theme at the Playhouse is California history. Pete explained that some panels’ cultural representations are not considered appropriate today. Those panels have been turn around and their blank backs are now seen. The walkers continued down Highland Avenue to Park Way, then turned around and walked to Hazel Lane. Other breads may be less sweet, so add sugar to your taste, up to another 1/4 cup. • Baking in a bain marie (hot • water bath) is optional. Direct baking (no water bath) works, but the bread pudding’s bottom and sides will brown and form a crust. Bread pudding is traditionally served with a crème anglaise. A super-premium ice cream has the same ingredients, so a shortcut is melting some ice cream. Strawberry Brioche Bread Pudding Makes 6–8 servings INGREDIENTS • 3 tablespoons unsalted butter, divided 1 tablespoon for the pan and 2 tablespoons to dot onto the bread pudding • 8 ounces brioche bread, about five 1+ inch thick slices • • • • • • • 3 extra large eggs 3 cups half and half, substitute 2 cups whole milk and 1 cup heavy cream (Avoid low fat milk in this recipe. It needs the richness for a creamy custard texture.) 1/4 cup granulated sugar 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 1/8 teaspoon sea salt 10 medium strawberries, halved. About 1-1/4 cups. Use very ripe fruit. Crème anglaise, or melted ice cream (see notes) INSTRUCTIONS Preheat oven to 300°F. Cut the brioche into 1-1/2 inch cubes. Spread in one layer on a 9” x 13” baking sheet and bake for about 5 minutes. Turn the cubes and bake for 3-ish minutes until they are dry, but still pale. Remove from the oven. This is all the baking for now. Butter a 2-quart, shallow baking dish (no taller than about 2-inches), with 1 tablespoon of butter. Transfer the bread cubes to the baking dish. Whisk the eggs, vanilla, sugar, and salt in a large bowl until the sugar is dissolved. Mix in the half and half. Pour over the bread cubes. Nestle the strawberries throughStrawberry Brioche Bread Pudding out. Press down gently for even absorption. Cover in plastic wrap and let soak in the refrigerator at least an hour or up to overnight. When ready to bake, bring the bread pudding to room temperature (or close). Once at room temperature, position an oven rack in the center position and preheat the oven to 350°F. Discard the plastic wrap then dot with bits of the remaining two tablespoons of butter. Cover tightly with aluminum foil. Cut a few slits in the top to vent. Place the bread pudding-filled casserole dish into a larger pan and fill the larger pan with hot water to halfway up the sides of Photo by Deborah Quok the casserole dish, creating a bain marie. Transfer both to the preheated oven. Avoid water splashing into the bread pudding. Bake covered for 40 minutes, then remove the foil and bake for 25–35 minutes until golden brown, fully puffy to the center. Test for doneness by inserting a clean, dry knife into the center of the pudding. It should come out clean (no eggy coating). Serve warm. Deborah Quok is the Piedmont Post’s longtime Food Editor. Karin Fetherston was interested in the historic ceiling panels in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School, and arranged for Pete Palmer, the school district’s Director of Facilities to meet the walkers at the and provide some history. Pete told the walkers about the ceiling, as well as needed repairs that were done to the building. Piedmont’s first public elementary school was built in 1910 and opened its doors in 19 . It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land donor. The school was expanded under the New Deal in the 1930s. After the school board gained funding from the Public Works Administration (PWA) in 1933, work on a new five-classroom wing and an auditorium on the eastern edge of the school began in 1936. The classrooms were built in 1937-38 and the auditorium was added in 1940-42. It was named in honor of Ellen Driscoll, the school’s first principal, who taught at the school for 20 years. The ceiling panels were painted by students in the fifth and sixth grade in a paint-by-number fashion before they were applied to the ceiling. The theme at the Playhouse is California history. Pete explained that some panels’ cultural representations are not considered appropriate today. Those panels have been turn around and their blank backs are now seen. The walkers continued down Highland Avenue to Park Way, then turned around and walked to Hazel Lane. At the turn of the twentieth century, Amy Requa Long wanted her daughters to have a good education, and she got Isaac Requa to build a oneroom schoolhouse on his property. Long hired a teacher for her daughters and a few neighborhood children. This was the very first school in Piedmont. Interest in the private school grew and in 1905 Amy leased a house at the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane, and hired Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges from the Anna Head School in Berkeley to be the new school’s teachers. The school attracted the daughters from many prominent Piedmont and early California families and soon outgrew its space. In 1908 Amy Long hired Julia Morgan to design a new school building with classrooms and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that is now Hazel Lane. The new Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls opened in 1913 for students from first grade through high school. In 1924 the school had 186 students and by 1928 it had 21 teachers and 42 graduating seniors. However, the Stock Market crash in 1929 and the following Depression created financial difficulties for many parents sending their daughters to the school. Piedmont High was less expensive and Ransom Bridges’ enrollment declined dramatically. In 1932 there were only 12 graduating seniors and the school closed in June that year. In 1936 the school building was demolished and the land developed by architect Albert Farr as Ransom Gardens. The group walked around the Hazel Lane loop to the school’s former site at 141 Hazel Lane. As they admired the home, the owner, Jody Cornelius, came out and talked with the walkers. The walkers completed the loop and took the hidden pathway on Hazel to Guildford Avenue and the town center to complete their fun 5th of July parade walk. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: On June 13, Piedmont Scout Troop 11 sent eight scouts, six boys, and two girls, with three adults, to a high adventure backpacking trek. The Scouts, ages 13 to 15, hiked Philmont Scout Ranch in Cimarron, New Mexico for 11 days, traversing over 80 miles with altitudes reaching nearly 12,000 ft. A ranger guided the crew for the first two days of the hike, coaching and reviewing skills needed to complete the trek, such as setting up camp in a “Bermuda Triangle” formation to avoid attracting bears. Then the Scouts were on their own to navigate the steep trails and high altitudes through the rugged New Mexico wilderness. Although the crew had planned for a 60-mile hike, they ultimately covered 80 miles due to additional day hikes. Provisions, including food and water, were carried by the Scouts, and stream water was filtered along the way for drinking. Most of the hike was mountainous but the terrain included dirt trails, large boulders, streams, and river crossings. They faced altitude challenges as they climbed, including reaching Mount Phillips, a 12,000-foot peak. They could see the devastation of the Ute Park fire in 2018 that burned more than 30,000 acres. To help with the restoration they participated in the Philmont conservation effort to rebuild trails. The Scouts also engaged in horseback riding, rock climbing, and fly fishing. At 6:45 a.m. on Wednesday, July 5, a man can be seen taking the inflatable off the float which was parked on Manor Drive. Surveillance photos further show him trying, but failing, to stuff the oversized corgi into his vehicle without deflating it. When the blow-up decoration wouldn’t fit, he decided to drive away with it, with a passenger holding it on the windshield.
